```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# ---- URPS workforce cross-reference (live from the mufflyaccess SSOT) -------
# The FPMRS/urogynecology footnote cites the 2023 board-certified-active URPS
# workforce from the canonical package (artifact contract 3.0.0) via urps_count(),
# never hardcoded. Fails loud if mufflyaccess is unavailable so the figure can
# never silently drift. NOTE: this makes mufflyaccess a render-time dependency.
if (!requireNamespace("mufflyaccess", quietly = TRUE))
  stop("mufflyaccess (>= 0.10.0) is required to render the URPS workforce cross-reference footnote.")
urps_ct <- function(include_urology, geography = "national")
  as.integer(mufflyaccess::urps_count(
    year = 2023L, measure = "board_certified_active",
    geography = geography, include_urology = include_urology, incomplete = "error"))

            identical(table1_year, figure1_year))

             "allsubspec_2020_inferential_TABLE.csv"))

  subspecialty == spec, group == grp)
fmt_p_txt <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "NA" else if (p < 0.001) "P<.001" else
  sub("=0\\.", "=.", sprintf(if (p < 0.01) "P=%.3f" else "P=%.2f", p))

# ---- formatters ------------------------------------------------------------
acc3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
acc2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pp1  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
en_dash <- function(x) gsub("(?<=[0-9])-(?=[0-9])", "-", x, perl = TRUE)
intc <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
# Strip the ACS interval from "X (lo-hi)", leaving the point estimate "X" (#7:
# independence makes pooled aggregate ratios' ACS intervals narrower than the
# reported precision, so they are presented as point estimates; see Methods).
point_only <- function(x) sub(" \\(.*\\)$", "", x)
gci  <- function(metric_name) {
  row <- dplyr::filter(go_ci_tbl, metric == metric_name)
  c(point = row$point, lo = row$lo, hi = row$hi)
}
gci_acc <- function(metric_name) {
  v <- gci(metric_name)
  sprintf("%s (95%% CI %s-%s)", acc3(v["point"]), acc3(v["lo"]),
          acc3(v["hi"]))
}
gci_pct <- function(metric_name) {
  v <- gci(metric_name)
  sprintf("%s%% (95%% CI %s-%s)", pp1(v["point"]), pp1(v["lo"]),
          pp1(v["hi"]))
}
spec_chg <- function(spec) dplyr::filter(change_tbl, subspecialty == spec)
spec_wk  <- function(spec) workforce_tbl$n_providers[
  workforce_tbl$subspecialty == spec]

# ---- cross-subspecialty equity summary (2020; drives the equity heatmap) ----
# Group-vs-reference percent difference in 2020 population-weighted access,
# WITHIN each subspecialty, from the canonical stratified series (same source
# behind Figures 3-6). Reference: rurality -> metropolitan; race -> White.
strat_long <- readr::read_csv(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "figures",
  "allsubspec_allyears_stratified_LONG.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
eq20 <- dplyr::filter(strat_long, year == 2020L)
.eq_pct <- function(subs, grp, refstrat) {
  g <- eq20$mean_access[eq20$subspec == subs & eq20$stratum == grp]
  r <- eq20$mean_access[eq20$subspec == subs & eq20$stratum == refstrat]
  100 * (g / r - 1)
}
subs7 <- E2SFCA_SUBSPECIALTIES   # SSOT: scripts/manuscript_e2sfca_values.R
rural_pct <- vapply(subs7, function(s) .eq_pct(s, "Rural", "Metropolitan"), 0)
aian_pct  <- vapply(subs7, function(s)
  .eq_pct(s, "Am. Indian/Alaska Native", "White, non-Hispanic"), 0)
n_rural_lower  <- sum(rural_pct < 0)          # lower access than metro
n_aian_worse   <- sum(aian_pct  < -10)        # materially (>=10%) lower than White
rural_worst    <- names(which.min(rural_pct)) # deepest rural penalty
rural_worst_pct <- min(rural_pct)
rural_min_pen  <- max(rural_pct)              # smallest rural penalty (closest to 0)

# ---- sensitivity analysis (2020 recompute under alternative assumptions) -----
# Canonical: scripts/sensitivity_e2sfca_2020.R re-ran every 2020 surface under
# alternative decay weights, catchment bands, and grid resolution.
sens_tbl  <- readr::read_csv(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "sensitivity",
  "sensitivity_2020.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sens_base <- dplyr::filter(sens_tbl, variant == "base")
sens_lab  <- c(base = "Sensitivity reference (1,000-m grid)",
  sharper = "Sharper distance decay", slower = "Slower distance decay",
  drop180 = "Drop 180-min band (30/60/120)",
  res500 = "Production resolution (500-m grid)",
  gaussian = "Gaussian distance decay (sigma = 60 min)",
  m2sfca = "M2SFCA maldistribution penalty")
# inline (mid-sentence) label forms: acronyms/proper nouns keep case, others lower
sens_lab_inline <- c(base = "reference specification",
  sharper = "sharper distance decay", slower = "slower distance decay",
  drop180 = "dropped 180-minute band", res500 = "production 500-m resolution",
  gaussian = "true Gaussian (sigma = 60 min)",
  m2sfca = "M2SFCA maldistribution penalty")
sens_summary <- purrr::map_dfr(setdiff(unique(sens_tbl$variant), "base"), function(vn) {
  vv <- dplyr::filter(sens_tbl, variant == vn)
  j  <- dplyr::inner_join(sens_base, vv, by = "subspec", suffix = c("_b", "_v"))
  tibble::tibble(variant = vn,
    rho = suppressWarnings(cor(j$national_b, j$national_v, method = "spearman")),
    rm_med = stats::median(vv$rural_metro_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),   # magnitude, not just direction
    aw_med = stats::median(vv$aian_white_ratio,  na.rm = TRUE),
    n_rural = sum(vv$rural_metro_ratio < 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_aian  = sum(vv$aian_white_ratio  < 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = nrow(vv))
})
sens_envelope <- sens_tbl |>
  dplyr::group_by(subspec) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_specs = dplyr::n_distinct(variant),
    rm_base = rural_metro_ratio[variant == "base"][1],
    rm_min = min(rural_metro_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    rm_max = max(rural_metro_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    rm_reversed = sum(rural_metro_ratio >= 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    aw_base = aian_white_ratio[variant == "base"][1],
    aw_min = min(aian_white_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    aw_max = max(aian_white_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    aw_reversed = sum(aian_white_ratio >= 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")
sens_env_rm_min <- min(sens_envelope$rm_min)
sens_env_rm_max <- max(sens_envelope$rm_max)
sens_env_aw_min <- min(sens_envelope$aw_min)
sens_env_aw_max <- max(sens_envelope$aw_max)
sens_env_any_rural_reversal <- any(sens_envelope$rm_reversed > 0)
sens_env_any_aian_reversal <- any(sens_envelope$aw_reversed > 0)
base_rm_med <- stats::median(sens_base$rural_metro_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)  # base rural:metro

# ---- self-referential word counts: computed LIVE at render, never hardcoded ----
# The precis is fully static, so its count is exact and single-sourced here:
precis_text <- paste(
  "Potential travel-time accessibility to board-certified obstetrics-gynecology",
  "subspecialists shows large, persistent rural and area-level racial disparities,",
  "worst in rural areas and in areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women live.")
precis_word_count <- length(strsplit(trimws(precis_text), "\\s+")[[1]])

# Abstract, main-text, and supplement counts are measured from the FINAL knitted
# markdown by a `document` hook (after inline code is evaluated) and substituted in
# for @@...@@ tokens, so a stale literal can never silently ship (cf. the 5,200-word
# drift). Exclusions mirror the audit counter: code, rendered tables, captions,
# citation keys, and subsection headings.
.wc_clean <- function(md) {
  md <- gsub("(?s)```.*?```", " ", md, perl = TRUE)         # fenced code
  md <- gsub("(?s)<table.*?</table>", " ", md, perl = TRUE) # rendered tables
  md <- gsub("(?s)<caption.*?</caption>", " ", md, perl = TRUE)
  md <- gsub("(?s)<!--.*?-->", " ", md, perl = TRUE)        # html comments
  md <- gsub("<[^>]+>", " ", md)                             # remaining html tags
  md <- gsub("\\[[-@;A-Za-z0-9 ]+\\]", " ", md)             # [@cite] keys
  md <- gsub("[#*_>`|]", " ", md)                            # markdown syntax
  md <- gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", md)
  w <- strsplit(trimws(md), " ")[[1]]; length(w[nzchar(w)])
}
.wc_section <- function(lines, start_re, stop_re) {
  h <- grep("^#{1,3} ", lines)
  st <- h[grepl(start_re, lines[h])]; if (!length(st)) return(NA_integer_)
  s <- st[1]; after <- h[h > s]
  sp <- after[grepl(stop_re, lines[after])]
  e <- if (length(sp)) sp[1] - 1L else length(lines)
  blk <- lines[(s + 1L):e]; blk <- blk[!grepl("^#{1,6} ", blk)]  # drop subsection headings
  .wc_clean(paste(blk, collapse = "\n"))
}
knitr::knit_hooks$set(document = function(x) {
  md <- paste(x, collapse = "\n"); L <- strsplit(md, "\n")[[1]]
  reps <- list(
    "@@ABSTRACT_WC@@" = .wc_section(L, "^#+ +Abstract", "^#+ +Introduction"),
    "@@MAIN_WC@@"     = .wc_section(L, "^#+ +Introduction",
                          "^#+ +(Supplemental Digital Content|Reproducibility|References)"),
    "@@SUPP_WC@@"     = .wc_section(L, "^#+ +Supplemental Digital Content",
                          "^#+ +(Reproducibility|References)"))
  for (tok in names(reps)) md <- gsub(tok, format(reps[[tok]], big.mark = ","), md, fixed = TRUE)
  md
})
```

```{r verbal-claim-guard, include=FALSE}
# ---- verbal quantifiers must agree with the numbers they describe -----------
# Every NUMBER in this paper is an inline R expression against the frozen run,
# so numbers cannot go stale. The WORDS around them can. "About one in five",
# "more than twice", "about six times" are hardcoded prose sitting next to
# computed values, and nothing tied the two together: re-freeze on a different
# run and the percentages update while the English silently does not.
#
# That is the same failure this project refuses everywhere else -- a result that
# looks fine and is quietly wrong -- so the claims are asserted here and a
# contradiction FAILS THE RENDER rather than shipping.
#
# Each rule states the arithmetic that makes the phrase honest, not merely a
# range someone found convenient. Change the phrase and you must change the rule
# with it; that is the point.
#
# Built as a plain list rather than a helper that accumulates with `<<-`: inside
# knitr the chunk body and any function defined in it do not share a parent, so
# `<<-` can write to a different binding than the check reads and the guard
# would silently never fire. Caught by negative-testing this guard, which is the
# only reason it is written this way.
.checks <- local({
  # "one in five" = 20%. A value earns that phrase when it is nearer 20% than
  # any other multiple of five, i.e. within 2.5 points.
  # One constant, used by both the test and the message, so the two can never
  # disagree about what the rule actually is.
  tol <- 2.5
  one_in_five <- function(x) isTRUE(abs(x - 20) <= tol)
  mrr    <- unname(gci("metro_rural_ratio")["point"])
  rz     <- unname(gci("rural_zero")["point"])
  mz     <- unname(gci("metro_zero")["point"])
  zratio <- rz / mz

  out <- list()
  for (s in c("GO", "MFM")) {
    v <- sp(s, "pct_outside_60")
    out[[length(out) + 1L]] <- list(
      ok = one_in_five(v),
      msg = sprintf("Abstract 'About one in five' (%s): outside 60 min is %.1f%%, not within %.1f points of 20%%", s, v, tol))
  }
  for (s in c("GO", "MFM", "FPMRS")) {
    v <- sp(s, "pct_outside_60")
    out[[length(out) + 1L]] <- list(
      ok = one_in_five(v),
      msg = sprintf("Results 'Roughly one in five' (%s): outside 60 min is %.1f%%, not within %.1f points of 20%%", s, v, tol))
  }
  # "more than twice the access" is a strict inequality, so check it as one.
  out[[length(out) + 1L]] <- list(
    ok = isTRUE(mrr > 2),
    msg = sprintf("Abstract 'more than twice the access': metro:rural access ratio is %.3f, not more than twice", mrr))
  # "about six times as likely": the rural:metro zero-access ratio must round to 6.
  # NB computed from the artifact, never from the rounded percentages printed in
  # the text -- 4.1/0.6 reads as 6.8 and would wrongly condemn a ratio of 6.45.
  out[[length(out) + 1L]] <- list(
    ok = isTRUE(abs(zratio - 6) <= 0.5),
    msg = sprintf("Abstract 'about six times as likely': rural:metro zero-access ratio is %.3f (%.4f%% vs %.4f%%), which does not round to six", zratio, rz, mz))
  attr(out, "summary") <- sprintf("metro:rural %.2fx, zero-access %.2fx", mrr, zratio)
  out
})

.bad <- vapply(.checks, function(z) !isTRUE(z$ok), logical(1))
if (any(.bad)) {
  stop(sprintf(
    "Manuscript verbal claims contradict their own computed values:\n  - %s\nEither the wording or the underlying run changed. Fix the sentence, or the rule above if the phrasing was deliberately revised.",
    paste(vapply(.checks[.bad], `[[`, character(1), "msg"), collapse = "\n  - ")),
    call. = FALSE)
}
message(sprintf("verbal-claim guard: %d claims checked, all consistent (%s)",
                length(.checks), attr(.checks, "summary")))
```

```{r diff-distance, include=FALSE}
# Complementary provider-referenced access metric (differential distance, Herb 2021):
# additional straight-line travel to the nearest urogynecologist (FPMRS) beyond the
# nearest general OB/GYN, women 65+. Source: scripts/urps_module_d_differential_distance.R.
```

## Abstract {-}

*Précis.* `r precis_text`

**Objective.** To measure geographic access to the seven obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialties across the contiguous United States, `r first_year` to `r last_year`,
and its disparities by rurality and by race and ethnicity.

**Methods.** We located every board-certified subspecialist active in each year and
measured reachability with modeled road-network drive times (30 to 180 minutes)
rather than straight-line distance for the 2020 female population
(`r intc(pop_2020)` women; American Community Survey). Potential accessibility was estimated with an
enhanced two-step floating catchment area model, which rewards shorter drives and
accounts for competing demand. We compared access by urban versus rural location and by race
and ethnicity, and described change from `r first_year` to `r primary_last`
(`r last_year` provisional).

**Results.** In 2020, geographic access was highly uneven. About one in five women lived more than a 60-minute drive from the nearest gynecologic oncology
(`r pp1(sp("GO","pct_outside_60"))`%) or maternal-fetal medicine
(`r pp1(sp("MFM","pct_outside_60"))`%) subspecialist, rising to
`r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_60"))`% for complex family planning; even within a
three-hour drive, `r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_180"))`% remained outside any
complex-family-planning catchment.
Metropolitan women had more than twice the access of rural women (gynecologic
oncology, `r acc2(gci("metro_rural_ratio")["point"])` times as much), and rural women
were about six times as likely to live where no subspecialist was located within the modeled catchment
(`r pp1(gci("rural_zero")["point"])`% vs `r pp1(gci("metro_zero")["point"])`%).
Areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived had the highest zero-access share
(`r pp1(gci("zero_aian")["point"])`%), `r pp1(gci("aianzero_minus_whitezero")["point"])`
points higher than areas where non-Hispanic White women lived. From `r first_year` to
`r primary_last`, minimally invasive gynecologic surgery increased most
(`r pp1(migs_c22$rel_change_pct)`%) and maternal-fetal medicine alone declined
(`r pp1(mfm_c22$rel_change_pct)`%). Rural disparities held across all
specifications.

**Conclusion.** Access to obstetrics-gynecology subspecialists shows large,
persistent rural and area-level racial disparities that narrowed little over the
decade. Across-subspecialty differences identify standardized geographic
reachability, not clinical adequacy, because every subspecialty was indexed to the
same total-female denominator.

```{r abstract-wordcount, results="asis"}
abstract_body <- paste(
  "Objective", "Methods", "Results", "Conclusion")  # labels excluded below
# count only rendered body words is done post-render; here note the source
cat(sprintf(
  "<!-- Abstract values sourced from run %s; allocator %s -->",
  manifest_json$run_id, manifest_json$allocator$method_id))
```

## Introduction

Access to advanced obstetric and gynecologic care depends not only on the size of
the workforce but also on where clinicians practice relative to the populations they
serve. The present study evaluates five subspecialties for which the American Board
of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) administers subspecialty certification, complex
family planning, gynecologic oncology, maternal-fetal medicine, reproductive
endocrinology and infertility, and urogynecology and reconstructive pelvic surgery,
and two areas with focused-practice designations, minimally invasive gynecologic
surgery and pediatric and adolescent gynecology. Prior studies suggest substantial
geographic concentration within individual fields: in 2020, 98.3% of gynecologic
oncologists practiced in urban areas [@Desjardins2023]; nearly 40% of
reproductive-aged women lived in areas with limited or no nearby access to assisted
reproductive technology services [@Harris2017]; and a national study of Indian Health
Service locations found a median drive time of 214 minutes to the nearest
obstetric-gynecologic subspecialist [@Akapo2023]. No previous study, however, has
compared potential travel-time accessibility across all seven fields using a common
national framework.

Although geographic proximity is only one of the five dimensions of health care
access [@Penchansky1981; @McLaughlin2002], travel burden influences whether and
when patients obtain care. Longer travel has been associated with less timely
prenatal care [@Deng2024], delays in abortion care [@Pleasants2022], limited
fertility treatment [@Harris2017], and, in oncology, delayed diagnosis and worse
outcomes [@Ambroggi2015], establishing travel time as a relevant barrier across
obstetric and gynecologic care [@Syed2013], while affordability, insurance,
appointment availability, and preferences also shape realized access.

Prior geographic-access research has focused largely on single subspecialties and on
straight-line or county-level distance. Desjardins and colleagues reported
county-level disparities in access to gynecologic oncologists over 2001-2020 with no
improvement for rural or American Indian or Alaska Native populations despite a
doubling of the workforce [@Desjardins2023]; Ackroyd and colleagues found
approximately 91% of U.S. counties with no practicing gynecologic oncologist
[@Ackroyd2021]. More broadly, nearly half of U.S. counties, roughly 20 million
people, lack any obstetrician-gynecologist [@Chen2026], and barely 1% of U.S. ZIP
codes contain a urogynecologist, with the greatest burden reported in places where
American Indian or Alaska Native women live [@Schmidt2024]. These studies characterize access as county-level
presence, a single travel-time threshold, or nearest-provider distance for one
service at a time, none accounting for the population competing for a given
subspecialist's time. The distance metric itself also matters. A geodesic
(straight-line) radius credits a woman with reaching a subspecialist she cannot
actually reach, because it ignores the road network, mountains, rivers, and coastlines
that lengthen the real trip; in a rural cohort, straight-line distance underestimated
true road distance by roughly a third on average and by as much as 83 miles in
individual cases [@Ludrosky2023], and the error is systematic rather than random,
concentrating in exactly the sparse-network rural areas where access is most in
question [@Apparicio2008]. Less is known about how potential accessibility compares across
the full set of OB/GYN subspecialties, how it has changed as the workforce entered,
retired, and relocated, and how it is distributed by rurality and by race and
ethnicity at a fine geographic scale.

We therefore estimated potential spatial accessibility to each of the seven specialty
groups across the contiguous United States from `r first_year` to `r last_year`,
using an enhanced two-step floating catchment area model on drive-time isochrones
routed over the road network, so that reachability is expressed in the currency a
patient actually spends, minutes behind the wheel, rather than in geodesic miles. We
characterized national accessibility levels and temporal trends by subspecialty and quantified disparities by rurality and by race and ethnicity, with
gynecologic oncology designated a priori as the detailed exemplar, both because timely
oncologic access is prognostically important and to permit comparison with existing
distance-based estimates [@Desjardins2023].

---

## Materials and Methods

### Study design and data sources

This was a retrospective, population-based geospatial analysis of potential
spatial accessibility to the seven American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology
(ABOG)-certified subspecialties across the 48 contiguous United States and the
District of Columbia, `r first_year` through `r last_year`. Population (demand) came
from U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates
[@Census2021ACS], retrieved with tidycensus [@Walker2024]; spatial operations used
the sf and terra frameworks [@Pebesma2018]. Only publicly available, de-identified
aggregate data were used; the study did not involve human participants and was exempt
from institutional review board review. [Author to confirm the reviewing IRB and
determination number.]

### Subspecialist cohort

For each calendar year, the analytic cohort comprised board-certified
subspecialists who were clinically active in that year. Subspecialty was assigned
from American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) board-certification
records, the certification standard used to define each subspecialty, rather than
from self-reported specialty codes, under which all obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialists are classified as generic obstetrics-gynecology.^[Because
subspecialty is ascertained from ABOG certification, the urogynecology and
reconstructive pelvic surgery (URPS) cohort counts only physicians certified
through the ABOG pathway; physicians who entered urogynecology through the
American Board of Urology (ABU) pathway are not captured. The 2020 URPS supply in
Table 1 is therefore a single-year, ABOG-only count. For 2023, the
board-certified active urogynecology workforce comprises `r intc(urps_ct(FALSE))`
physicians through the ABOG pathway and `r intc(urps_ct(TRUE) - urps_ct(FALSE))`
ABU net-new physicians (`r intc(urps_ct(TRUE))` nationally and
`r intc(urps_ct(TRUE, "conus"))` in the contiguous United States); the difference
from the 2020 figure reflects the later measure year and the added ABU pathway
rather than a difference in ascertainment.] A physician was
counted as clinically active in year *Y* when their estimated retirement year
exceeded *Y* (strict inequality; retirement was estimated from a multi-source
consensus of practice-activity signals, and certification dated entry to the
subspecialty), and was placed at their practice location for that year, so each
contributed to a subspecialty's surface only while active. No physician-year showed
multiple concurrent locations, so no supply was double-counted (eMethods).
Physicians were included only if their practice address geocoded to a
contiguous-U.S. location. Each specialty group's supply is therefore a geocoded,
contiguous-U.S., clinically-active count, smaller than a board-certification
headcount, which counts all certificants regardless of clinical activity, geocoding,
or location. In `r table1_year`,
`r intc(sum(workforce_tbl$n_providers))` subspecialists were active across the seven
specialty groups (Table 1), and the panel comprises `r nrow(national_tbl)`
specialty-year cells (`r n_subspec` groups × `r n_years` years).

### Population, denominators, and geographic units

The demand denominator was the total female population by census tract (ACS table
B01001), applied identically to all seven subspecialties to yield a standardized
index; because the subspecialties serve different age ranges (for example, pediatric
and adolescent gynecology serves children and adolescents, whereas urogynecology
serves a predominantly older population), across-subspecialty rate comparisons
reflect workforce size and clinical scope in addition to access (Discussion). For
race and ethnicity, non-Hispanic White (ACS table B01001H) and Hispanic-origin (any
race; B01001I) women were analyzed alongside race-alone groups (Black, Asian,
American Indian or Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander;
B01001B-E); because race-alone counts can include persons of Hispanic origin, these
are separately defined groups, not a mutually exclusive partition. Rurality used U.S.
Department of Agriculture Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes [@usda_ruca], with
primary codes 1-3 metropolitan and 4-10 rural. Census tract vintage changed between
2019 and 2020 (`r first_year`-2019 on 2010-vintage tracts, 2020-`r last_year` on
2020-vintage, each with contemporaneous ACS estimates); a prespecified seam analysis
showed negligible effects on the national estimates, and a subgroup seam test holding
the 2020 cohort fixed found the vintage-induced shift small for every group (median
`r sprintf("%.2f", seam_zero_med)` percentage point in the zero-access share, at most
`r pp1(seam_ra_max)` for rural areas or areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived and
`r pp1(seam_zero_max)` overall; mean-access shift ≤`r acc3(seam_mean_max)` per
100,000), so the subgroup trends are not vintage artifacts (Discussion; eMethods S3).
Alaska's exclusion is relevant to the American Indian or Alaska Native findings
(Discussion). The 2020 analysis represented `r intc(pop_2020)` women.

### Travel-time isochrones

Drive-time isochrones of 30, 60, 120, and 180 minutes were generated around each
physician location with the Valhalla routing engine on OpenStreetMap road networks
[@Valhalla2023]. The network was held constant across study years (a single
OpenStreetMap snapshot; *[extract date to be confirmed by the authors]*), so
year-to-year change in the accessible footprint reflects only the change in the
active cohort, not the road extract.

Reachability was defined by drive time rather than by geodesic (straight-line)
distance, a substantive rather than technical choice. A straight-line buffer is a
circle; the set of places from which a physician can actually be reached in a fixed
time is not, because roads bend around mountains, water, and roadless land, and
because a mile of two-lane surface road is not a mile of interstate
[@Apparicio2008; @Ebinger2022]. The divergence is largest where the network is
sparse, so a geodesic measure credits rural women with access they do not have and
biases the very rural-urban contrast this study estimates [@Ludrosky2023]. Drive time
is also the impedance in which the model's distance-decay weights were originally
estimated, and the one in which referral and travel decisions are actually made
(eMethods S4).

### Enhanced two-step floating catchment area accessibility

We measured access with the enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA)
method [@luoqi2009; @luowang2003], a standard way to estimate how reachable a
service is once both travel distance and competition are taken into account. It combines two questions. First, for each subspecialist, how many
women live within driving range, and therefore compete for that physician's time?
Second, for each neighborhood, how many subspecialists lie within driving range,
after each is discounted by the demand he or she already serves? Providers a woman
can reach quickly count more than ones hours away. The result is a single number for
every location, the subspecialists effectively available per 100,000 women, scaled
so the national average equals 1.00 [@Wan2012spar].

One feature matters for interpretation: the national average is mathematically just
the total subspecialists divided by the total population, so we report it only as a
standardized measure of workforce size, not of geographic access. The access signal
lies in how the index is *distributed*, whether rural and urban women and different
racial and ethnic groups can reach a subspecialist and how much of the population
lies outside any subspecialist's reach; those distributional measures are our primary
outcomes. The travel-time weights, formulas, and sensitivity tests are in eMethods S4.

### Mass-conserving demand allocation

To line up the physician catchments with where women live, we spread each census
tract's female population across a fine 500-m national grid in proportion to land
area, so every tract's population total was preserved (`r cons_pct(cons_loss_area)`%
lost, versus `r cons_pct(cons_loss_centroid)`% when a tract is collapsed to a single
center point); a coarser 1,000-m grid gave nearly identical results. This assumes
population is spread evenly within a tract, an approximation that is weakest in large
rural and tribal tracts (eMethods S2).

### Temporal comparison

The `r first_year`-`r last_year` comparison surfaces were computed on a single common grid and denominator (2020 vintage; ACS 2020) so the difference reflects only the change in the active cohort (eMethods S3).

### Statistical analysis

National accessibility was summarized as the population-weighted mean; because the
physician catchments are deterministic and tracts were treated as independent,
ACS-only intervals are near-zero-width and are reported as ACS sampling intervals,
not comprehensive confidence intervals. We separately quantified a deterministic
model-specification envelope for the main 2020 disparity ratios across the
sensitivity specifications. Temporal change was summarized by ordinary least-squares
slopes with Newey-West HAC P values, excluding the most recent (right-censored) year;
stratified trend analyses are exploratory. The uncertainty model, zero-access
estimators, trend specification, and robustness analyses are detailed in eMethods S1.
Analyses used R version `r manifest_json$environment$r_version`.

### Quality assurance and validation

Every surface was subjected to an automated validation battery, and the analysis is reproducible from a version-controlled, hash-verified run. Builds are deterministic: independent reruns from identical inputs reproduce the raster surfaces byte-for-byte, verified by SHA-256 content hashes recorded in the frozen run manifest alongside the producing source commit, so any change to a reported value is detectable rather than silent. Automated geographic-integrity checks confirm conservation of census-tract counts, preservation of tract topology across the 2010-to-2020 vintage transition (isolated by the seam analysis above), continuity across state and tract seams, and land-clipping of coastal and water tracts. Provider-to-catchment coverage was verified with a distance-based matcher rather than exact coordinate matching, and the analytic scope was enforced to the contiguous United States at defined filter points. Record linkages among the certification, activity, and geography sources were guarded against one-to-many fan-out, and estimates were cross-checked against independent reference computations and state-by-state visual audits of the accessibility surfaces.

---

## Results

### Subspecialist workforce and study population

We modeled potential spatial accessibility to board-certified obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialists active in each year from `r first_year` through `r last_year`, for the
`r intc(pop_2020)` women represented by the 2020 American Community Survey
[@Census2021ACS]. In `r table1_year`, the active
workforce comprised `r intc(spec_wk("MFM"))` maternal-fetal medicine (MFM),
`r intc(spec_wk("GO"))` gynecologic oncology (GO), `r intc(spec_wk("REI"))`
reproductive endocrinology and infertility (REI), `r intc(spec_wk("FPMRS"))`
urogynecology and reconstructive pelvic surgery (URPS),
`r intc(spec_wk("MIGS"))` minimally invasive gynecologic surgery (MIGS),
`r intc(spec_wk("PAG"))` pediatric and adolescent gynecology (PAG), and
`r intc(spec_wk("CFP"))` complex family planning (CFP) physicians (Table 1).

```{r table1}
abbr_note <- paste0("AIAN, American Indian or Alaska Native; CFP, complex family ",
  "planning; GO, ",
  "gynecologic oncology; MFM, maternal-fetal medicine; MIGS, minimally invasive ",
  "gynecologic surgery; PAG, pediatric and adolescent gynecology; REI, ",
  "reproductive endocrinology and infertility; URPS, urogynecology and ",
  "reconstructive pelvic surgery.")
tbl1 <- workforce_tbl |>
  dplyr::transmute(subspecialty, physicians = n_providers) |>
  dplyr::left_join(national_tbl |> dplyr::filter(year == table1_year) |>
    dplyr::transmute(subspecialty, access = mean_pop_weighted_per100k),
    by = "subspecialty") |>
  dplyr::left_join(change_tbl_22 |>
    dplyr::transmute(subspecialty, relc = rel_change_pct), by = "subspecialty") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(access)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Subspecialty = full_name_disp[subspecialty],
    `Active, non-federal, patient care physicians, 2020` = formatC(physicians, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `Supply per 100,000 women (all ages), 2020` = sprintf("%.3f", access),
    `Change, 2013-2022` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", relc))
knitr::kable(tbl1, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = paste0("Table 1. Active Workforce and Standardized Supply per ",
    "Population by Obstetrics-Gynecology Subspecialty, ", table1_year)) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
                            font_size = 12, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "Counts are active, non-federal, patient care physicians in ", table1_year, ", defined here ",
    "as board-certified subspecialists clinically active that year and geocoded to ",
    "a contiguous-U.S. practice location. The supply-per-population column is the national ",
    "population-weighted mean of the enhanced two-step floating catchment area ",
    "surface, which by a property of the method equals subspecialist ",
    "supply per 100,000 women (Methods); it is a standardized ",
    "workforce-distribution index, not a spatial-accessibility measure, and its ",
    "ranking is the workforce-size ranking. Spatial distribution and disparities ",
    "are reported in Tables 2-3 and Figures 3-6. Change is the ",
    "descriptive relative change from ", first_year, " to ",
    primary_last, "; ", last_year, " is right-censored and reported provisionally. ",
    "Trend inference is given in Appendix Table S1. ", abbr_note))
```

### Spatial distribution and inequality of access

Because the national mean carries no spatial information (Methods), we describe the
*geographic distribution* of access. In 2020, potential accessibility concentrated in
metropolitan areas of the eastern and midwestern United States, with large regions of
the Mountain West and Great Plains outside any subspecialist's catchment; the scarcest
fields, complex family planning and pediatric and adolescent gynecology, showed
extensive zero-access areas across most land outside major metros (Figure 1).

```{r figlevel}
# Figure 1 provenance: isochrones scripts/map_allsubspec_level_2020_faceted.R
# (built 2026-07-15; regenerated 2026-08-02). See docs/FIGURE_PROVENANCE.md.
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig0_level2020.jpg"))
```
**Figure 1.** Potential spatial accessibility to each obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialty, 2020, per 100,000 women, estimated with an enhanced
two-step floating catchment area model on 30-, 60-, 120-, and 180-minute
travel-time isochrones. Brighter shading indicates greater potential accessibility;
black indicates no modeled access (a desert). One panel per subspecialty on a
shared square-root color scale (capped at the 98th percentile); the number in each
label is the national population-weighted mean. Mass-conserving 500-m demand grid
aggregated to a 1,000-m display surface; contiguous United States.

Roughly one in five women in 2020 lived
outside a 60-minute drive of the nearest subspecialist for the more common
fields, `r pp1(sp("GO","pct_outside_60"))`% for gynecologic oncology,
`r pp1(sp("MFM","pct_outside_60"))`% for maternal-fetal medicine, and
`r pp1(sp("FPMRS","pct_outside_60"))`% for urogynecology and reconstructive pelvic surgery, rising to
`r pp1(sp("PAG","pct_outside_60"))`% for pediatric and adolescent gynecology and
`r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_60"))`% for complex family planning (Table 2). Even
within a three-hour drive, `r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_180"))`% of women remained
outside any complex-family-planning catchment and `r pp1(sp("PAG","pct_outside_180"))`%
outside any pediatric and adolescent gynecology catchment, versus
`r pp1(sp("GO","pct_outside_180"))`% for gynecologic oncology. By the population-weighted Gini index, concentration was lowest for
`r full_name[sp_gini_min_sub]` (`r acc2(sp_gini_min)`) and highest for
`r full_name[sp_gini_max_sub]` (`r acc2(sp_gini_max)`), so the scarcest fields are not
only smaller but far more unevenly distributed (Table 2).

```{r table2sp}
sp_tab <- spatial_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(subspec = factor(subspec,
    levels = E2SFCA_SUBSPECIALTIES)) |>   # SSOT display order
  dplyr::arrange(subspec) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Subspecialty = full_name_disp[subspec],
    `% outside 60 min` = sprintf("%.1f", pct_outside_60),
    `% outside 120 min` = sprintf("%.1f", pct_outside_120),
    `% outside 180 min` = sprintf("%.1f", pct_outside_180),
    `Gini` = sprintf("%.2f", gini))
knitr::kable(sp_tab, align = c("l","r","r","r","r"),
  caption = paste0("Table 2. Spatial Distribution and Inequality of Potential ",
    "Accessibility by Subspecialty, 2020")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","condensed"),
                            font_size = 12, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "“% outside t min” is the share of women with no subspecialist ",
    "reachable within a t-minute drive (population-weighted, road-network ",
    "travel time). Gini is the population-weighted Gini index of the accessibility ",
    "surface (0 = perfectly even; higher = more spatially concentrated). These are ",
    "spatial-distribution measures and, unlike the standardized supply index in ",
    "Table 1, depend on provider geography. Computed on a 1-km demand grid. ",
    abbr_note))
```

The standardized supply index (Table 1) was highest for maternal-fetal medicine and
lowest for complex family planning (Figure 2A); because it equals workforce supply
per population (Methods), it reflects workforce size and clinical scope, not spatial
access, and is not comparable across subspecialties.

```{r fig1}

# also vendored in twostep/scripts/). See docs/FIGURE_PROVENANCE.md.
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig1_national.jpg"))
```
**Figure 2.** National potential accessibility to OB/GYN subspecialists,
`r first_year`-`r last_year` (E2SFCA on travel-time isochrones). (A)
Population-weighted accessibility by subspecialty, 2020. (B) By subspecialty,
`r first_year`-`r last_year` (log scale). Cell-level population-weighted; per
100,000 women.

### Temporal trends

From `r first_year` to `r primary_last` (the primary period; `r last_year` was
right-censored and is reported provisionally), minimally invasive gynecologic
surgery increased from `r acc3(migs_c22[["y2013"]])` to
`r acc3(migs_c22[[paste0("y", primary_last)]])` per 100,000 women (a
`r pp1(migs_c22$rel_change_pct)`% relative change), the largest relative increase
among the subspecialties, and maternal-fetal medicine was the only subspecialty to
decline (`r acc3(mfm_c22[["y2013"]])` to
`r acc3(mfm_c22[[paste0("y", primary_last)]])`; `r pp1(mfm_c22$rel_change_pct)`%).
Gynecologic oncology increased from
`r acc3(go_c22[["y2013"]])` to `r acc3(go_c22[[paste0("y", primary_last)]])`
(`r pp1(go_c22$rel_change_pct)`%; Figure 2B). On a provisional basis, minimally invasive gynecologic surgery reached
`r acc3(migs_c[["y2023"]])` and maternal-fetal medicine `r acc3(mfm_c[["y2023"]])`
per 100,000 women in `r last_year`.

### Disparities by rurality

For gynecologic oncology in 2020, population-weighted accessibility was
`r acc2(gci("metro_mean")["point"])` per 100,000 women in metropolitan
areas versus `r acc2(gci("rural_mean")["point"])` in rural areas, a
metropolitan-to-rural ratio of `r acc2(gci("metro_rural_ratio")["point"])`
(Figure 3A; ACS uncertainty intervals for all estimates appear in Table 3). At the
extreme of no access, `r pp1(gci("rural_zero")["point"])`% of rural women lived in a tract with zero mean modeled access to a gynecologic oncologist, versus `r pp1(gci("metro_zero")["point"])`% of metropolitan women, roughly sixfold higher.

### Disparities by race and ethnicity

Areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived had the lowest gynecologic
oncology accessibility (`r acc3(gci("mean_aian")["point"])` per 100,000) and the
highest share of group population in census tracts with zero mean modeled access
(`r pp1(gci("zero_aian")["point"])`%); the zero-access share was
`r pp1(gci("aianzero_minus_whitezero")["point"])` percentage points higher than for
areas where non-Hispanic White women lived (ACS uncertainty interval excluding zero).
Areas where Asian women lived had the highest modeled accessibility (Figure 3B).

**Figure 3.** Population-weighted 2020 accessibility to the seven OB/GYN
subspecialties by (A) rurality and (B) race and ethnicity, per 100,000 women;
subspecialties ordered by national mean. In (A) each line joins the rural and
metropolitan means; in (B) each point is one group, spanning the lowest to the
highest. Rurality is USDA RUCA 2020 (metropolitan = codes 1 to 3); race-alone groups
are not mutually exclusive with the non-Hispanic White and Hispanic groups. AIAN,
American Indian or Alaska Native; NHPI, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander;
URPS, urogynecology and reconstructive pelvic surgery.

### Disparities across all subspecialties

The rurality and area-level race/ethnicity disparities held across all seven specialty groups (Figure 3), with rural areas and areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived lowest in every one; per-subspecialty estimates are in eResults S5.

### Persistence of disparities over time

The rural and area-level racial disparities persisted with little narrowing across `r first_year`-`r last_year`; the year-by-year detail is in eResults S6.

### Access deserts across subspecialties

The share of women outside any modeled catchment ("access deserts") varied widely by subspecialty; per-subspecialty values are in eResults S7.

---

### Change in accessibility by subspecialty

Decade-scale change differed by subspecialty, minimally invasive gynecologic surgery increased most and maternal-fetal medicine alone declined; the per-subspecialty change is in eResults S8.

## Discussion

In this national analysis of potential spatial accessibility to the seven
ABOG-certified obstetric-gynecologic subspecialties, accessibility concentrated in
metropolitan areas and was lowest for rural areas and for areas where American Indian
or Alaska Native women lived, changing little across the study period. The
subspecialties differed markedly in standardized geographic reachability and temporal
trajectories, but those cross-subspecialty differences should not be read as
differences in clinical adequacy because the denominator was the same total female
population for every field.

Our findings extend prior single-subspecialty and county-level work. For gynecologic
oncology, our results refine the county-level model of Desjardins and colleagues, who
found 95.2% of counties (roughly 54.7 million at-risk women) with no gynecologic
oncologist and no improvement over two decades for American Indian or Alaska Native
women beyond 100 miles (25.6% to 23.7%; P=.866) [@Desjardins2023]. Our smaller
board-certified cohort makes counts not directly comparable, but our travel-time,
tract-level surface corroborates the same inequities across all seven groups. A
state-level E2SFCA analysis similarly found 18.4% of Georgia tracts with zero access
[@Graham2019], the logic behind our stratified synthesis (Figure 4).

A provider-referenced metric reinforces this for urogynecology: the extra travel to
the nearest urogynecologist beyond the nearest general obstetrician-gynecologist
[@Herb2021]. Women 65 or older in the median county faced roughly `r diff_median_mi`
additional miles, and `r diff_pct_gt30`% faced more than 30, evidence that
subspecialty maldistribution, not an absence of gynecologic care, drives the rural
gap.

Our other-subspecialty findings are likewise consistent with the literature: the
extensive reproductive endocrinology and infertility deserts echo estimates that
roughly 29% of reproductive-aged women lack a nearby assisted reproductive technology
clinic, with documented racial and ethnic disparities [@Beroukhim2023], and an
oncofertility analysis found the share beyond a two-hour drive nearly doubled from
general to subspecialized care (3.4% to 5.7%) [@Peipert2023]. Such disparities are
multifactorial, extending beyond structural access [@Seifer2022].

This persistence mirrors access gradients across many specialized services, from
cardiac rehabilitation and transplantation to cancer, mental health, and
rehabilitation care, where rural and American Indian or Alaska Native populations are
consistently farther from care [@Ebinger2022; @Yilma2023; @Liu2023; @Towne2014;
@ElKhoury2024; @Hecox2026; @Welch2024; @Campbell2025; @Charlesworth2024]; the most
comparable, a national E2SFCA analysis of six dental specialties, reproduced our
patterns, with more than 98% of specialists urban and rural people driving roughly
three times as far [@Rahman2026].
Because subspecialists cluster in metropolitan academic and referral centers, many
rural and American Indian or Alaska Native areas lie beyond even a 180-minute drive
of any, so workforce growth alone need not reach them; indeed the workforce grew
while their access held nearly constant. Because
the denominator is total population rather than disease or procedure demand, these
estimates locate where the geographic component of access is most deficient, not
where clinical need is greatest. Narrowing the gaps therefore likely requires
strategies that decouple access from physician relocation, hub-and-spoke models,
telehealth, knowledge-sharing networks such as Project ECHO [@Arora2023], placement
incentives, and visiting-specialist clinics, each warranting evaluation rather than
presumed benefit.

Potential accessibility is not a surrogate for realized use: of the five dimensions
of access, the model captures only availability and geographic accessibility
[@Penchansky1981; @McLaughlin2002], not affordability, accommodation, or
acceptability. Populations with high modeled proximity can still fare poorly, facing
systemic racism, insurance and scheduling barriers, and higher disease burden
[@Bassett2020]. The metropolitan concentration mirrors the race-by-rurality intersection
reported for emergency surgery [@McCrum2022] and mammography [@Campbell2026];
because racial outcome disparities attenuate after adjustment for insurance, income,
and education [@Greenberg2023], a geographic difference becomes an inequity when
patterned by unequally distributed social factors [@Hod2014]. Modeled proximity is
thus necessary but insufficient for equitable care.

Strengths include a near-census of board-certified subspecialists rather than a
sample; a mass-conserving demand allocation representing the full female population
[@Apparicio2017]; year-specific cohorts reflecting workforce entry, exit, and
relocation; and fully reproducible, canonical-source computation. Unlike
nearest-provider travel time or provider ratios, the floating-catchment design jointly
incorporates provider availability, competing demand, and travel impedance, flagging
low-access areas those simpler measures miss [@Drake2021].

Measuring impedance as drive time rather than geodesic distance is a particular
strength here. The literature this study extends is largely geodesic or areal, a
100-mile radius [@Desjardins2023], provider presence in a county [@Ackroyd2021;
@Chen2026] or ZIP code [@Schmidt2024], or straight-line differential distance
[@Herb2021], each treating a mile of interstate and a mile of switchback mountain
road as the same barrier. Straight-line distance understated true road distance by
about a third in a rural cohort [@Ludrosky2023], and because that error is
directionally consistent it does not merely add noise to a rural-urban comparison but
should compress it, so the disparities reported here are likely conservative relative
to a geodesic measure. A nationwide comparison found the two metrics nearly
interchangeable for non-emergency trips to community hospitals [@Boscoe2012], but
that describes short trips to a dense, ubiquitous facility type; the gap between
geodesic and road distance widens with trip length and network sparsity, which is the
regime a subspecialty analysis occupies. Drive time also makes the catchment bands
operationally meaningful: 30 to 180 minutes maps onto referral, day-trip, and
overnight travel in a way a mileage ring does not. The trade-off is that drive time
inherits modeling assumptions a geodesic measure does not make (eDiscussion S9); the
full argument is in eMethods S4.

Several limitations temper interpretation. The common total-female-population denominator makes across-subspecialty comparisons reflect workforce size and clinical scope as well as access, so these standardized indices should not be read as direct measures of clinical adequacy; the index measures potential rather than realized access and omits practice capacity, appointment availability, insurance, and patient travel behavior; the reported intervals capture only ACS sampling error; the zero-access metric is tract-level; race-alone and Hispanic-origin groups are not mutually exclusive; the race/ethnicity contrasts are ecological descriptions of the areas where groups live, not individual-level causal effects; and Alaska's exclusion limits generalizability to Alaska Native communities with distinct transportation barriers. These points, with international-border edge effects, the uniform-within-tract density assumption, and directions for patient-flow calibration, are detailed in eDiscussion S9.

## Conclusion

Across the contiguous United States, potential accessibility to board-certified
obstetric and gynecologic subspecialists was persistently lower in rural areas and
in areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived, and narrowed little
over more than a decade.
As a measure of where specialized care is potentially reachable, not of realized or
clinically sufficient access, these findings identify the populations and regions
that may benefit most from regionalized care, outreach, telehealth, and targeted
workforce strategies.

---

## Supplemental Digital Content {-}


## eMethods S1: Statistical analysis {-}

National accessibility was summarized as the population-weighted mean at the
raster-cell level. We report two quantified uncertainty layers. First, ACS
uncertainty intervals reflect sampling error in the population weights: because the
physician catchments and cell-level accessibility values are deterministic (a
near-census of active physicians on fixed isochrones), we propagated the ACS margins
of error by Monte-Carlo simulation (2,000 draws; each tract's female population
drawn from a Normal distribution with SD = margin of error ÷ 1.645) and summarized
each estimate by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
Draws were not truncated at zero: because they enter only aggregate weighted sums
(where the expectation equals the sum of the tract estimates), clamping would inject
spurious positive weight into the many zero-population tracts and bias sparse groups
(for example, American Indian or Alaska Native) upward. Tracts were treated as
independent, so the variance of an aggregate is the sum of tract variances; this
does not use the ACS covariance structure or replicate weights, and because errors
average out across the tens of thousands of tracts, the intervals for pooled
quantities, especially aggregate ratios such as the metropolitan-to-rural ratio,
collapse to implausibly narrow ranges. Such intervals should be read as ACS-only
intervals rather than comprehensive confidence intervals; we accordingly report a
point estimate alone where the interval is narrower than the reported precision.
Second, we report a deterministic model-specification envelope across the
prespecified 2020 sensitivity specifications (Appendix Tables S2-S2b), spanning
distance-decay weights, the 180-minute catchment, grid resolution, Gaussian-derived
zonal weights, and an M2SFCA maldistribution penalty. This envelope is not a
probability interval, but it quantifies how much the main rurality and AIAN-vs-White
contrasts move under plausible modeling choices. It still does not incorporate
stochastic uncertainty from physician ascertainment, clinical-activity
classification, geocoding, multiple practice locations, practice capacity, or
road-network travel-time modeling. Rurality- and race/ethnicity-stratified estimates were computed
at the tract level (required to attach RUCA rurality and race-specific
denominators) and reconcile with the cell-level national summary to within 0.001
per 100,000 women. The zero-access metric (“% zero”) is the share of a
group’s population living in census tracts whose mean modeled access is zero. As a
sensitivity comparison, we also computed a cell-level estimator for 2020, the
area-weighted share of each tract lying in grid cells with zero access, weighted by
the tract's group population, which was stable between the 500-m and 1,000-m grids
(agreement within 0.1 percentage point for the subspecialties checked) and gave
higher zero-access shares than the tract-mean definition (Appendix Table S3).
Because both estimators rest on the same area-weighted (uniform within-tract
density) allocation, this difference reflects the choice of definition, not
independent evidence that either value is more accurate; a dasymetric or block-level
allocation would be required to establish that (Discussion). A subspecialist was considered reachable if the practice location
fell within the 180-minute maximum travel-time catchment. Temporal change was
summarized by ordinary least-squares slopes of the annual estimate on calendar year
over `r first_year`-`r primary_last`. Because successive ACS 5-year estimates
overlap and provider cohorts are serially correlated, we also computed Newey-West
heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) P values, with the lag
prespecified at `r trend_hac$hac_lag` to reflect the overlap of the 5-year ACS
window (Appendix Table S1); because only 10 annual estimates were available, these
trend tests are imprecise and are interpreted descriptively. The stratified trend
analyses across the seven specialty groups and multiple groups are exploratory: we
prespecified no primary comparison and applied no multiple-comparisons correction,
and we therefore emphasize the direction and magnitude of change over statistical
significance. The most recent year (`r last_year`) was excluded from trend
estimation and is reported as a provisional observation because its workforce panel
is subject to right-censoring. To assess robustness to modeling choices, we
recomputed the 2020 accessibility surface for every subspecialty under the
alternative specifications summarized in Appendix Table S2, and compared the national
ranking and the rurality and race contrasts with the base specification.
Analyses used R version `r manifest_json$environment$r_version`.

## eMethods S2: Mass-conserving demand allocation {-}

Demand was allocated from census tracts to a 500-m equal-area analysis grid
(EPSG:5070) by polygon-cell area overlap, conserving every tract's population
(mass-conserving area-weighted allocation). This preserved each tract's modeled
population total (`r cons_pct(cons_loss_area)`% loss) versus a `r cons_pct(cons_loss_centroid)`% loss under conventional centroid-based
allocation; per-year national totals were conserved to within 10⁻⁶. Conserving
population prevents the loss that centroid allocation incurs and reduces the
display-scale aggregation that coarser zone centroids impose [@BryantDelamater2019];
it does not, however, improve the underlying spatial precision, because population
is distributed by land-area overlap and the method therefore assumes uniform
population density within each tract. This assumption is least tenable in large
rural and tribal tracts, where women occupy a small fraction of the land area,
so the 500-m surface can appear more spatially precise than the tract-level input
justifies (see Limitations). The 500-m and 1,000-m surfaces nonetheless gave
near-identical results (Appendix Table S2).

## eMethods S3: Temporal comparison, 2013-2023 {-}

National accessibility was computed for every subspecialty-year cell. To visualize
decade-scale change while isolating the cohort effect, the `r first_year` and
`r last_year` accessibility surfaces for each subspecialty were computed on a
single common grid and demand denominator (2020 tract vintage; ACS 2020), so the
difference reflects only the change in the active physician cohort.


*Appendix 1. Accessibility change by subspecialty, `r first_year`-`r last_year`
(to be posted online as Supplemental Digital Content).*

Level maps look similar year-to-year because the workforce is ~85-95% persistent
between consecutive years; the change accumulates. To isolate the cohort signal,
each figure below computes the `r first_year` and `r last_year` surfaces on one
common grid (2020 tract vintage; ACS 2020), so the difference (panel C) reflects
only the change in the active physician cohort. Red = access grew; blue = shrank.
Because both years are placed on the 2020 grid, the national means and percentage
changes annotated on these figures are computed on that common (cohort-isolated)
basis. The primary temporal changes reported in the Results and Table 1 use
`r first_year` to `r primary_last` (the last complete reporting year, because
`r last_year` is right-censored and provisional; e.g., minimally invasive
gynecologic surgery `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", spec_chg22("MIGS")$rel_change_pct)`,
maternal-fetal medicine `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", spec_chg22("MFM")$rel_change_pct)`).
These appendix change maps and Figure 7 instead display the full `r first_year`-to-
`r last_year` endpoint difference (minimally invasive gynecologic surgery
`r sprintf("%+.0f%%", migs_c$rel_change_pct)`, maternal-fetal medicine
`r sprintf("%+.0f%%", mfm_c$rel_change_pct)`), with `r last_year` as a provisional
endpoint; they show the underlying spatial pattern over the full study window and
therefore differ from the primary `r first_year`-to-`r primary_last` estimates.

*Appendix 2. Sensitivity of the 2020 findings to modeling assumptions.*

The 2020 accessibility surface for each subspecialty was recomputed under
alternative distance-decay weights (sharper and slower falloff than the base
weights, and a true Gaussian with sigma = 60 min), an M2SFCA maldistribution
penalty, a reduced catchment that dropped the 180-minute band, and the
production 500-m grid (the sensitivity was computed on a 1,000-m reference grid for
efficiency; the 500-m specification reproduces the resolution that generated the
production national values). The national population-weighted mean and its induced
subspecialty ranking were identical across every specification (Spearman
`r if (sens_rho_identical) "ρ = 1.00" else sprintf("ρ ≥ %.2f", sens_min_rho)`); this
is *not* evidence of spatial robustness but a direct consequence of the conservation
property (Methods), the national mean equals supply divided by population and does
not depend on the decay weights, catchment bands, or grid resolution. The meaningful
sensitivity is therefore in the *spatial* quantities. Rural women had lower
accessibility
than metropolitan women for all `r sens_n` subspecialties under every
specification. Areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived had lower
accessibility than areas where non-Hispanic White women lived for all `r sens_n`
subspecialties under the
base, sharper-decay, true-Gaussian, dropped-band, and production-resolution
specifications, and for `r min(sens_summary$n_aian)` of `r sens_n` under the
slowest decay and the M2SFCA maldistribution penalty (complex family
planning, already near parity, crossed to a slight advantage). Magnitudes did move, and Table S2
reports them: the median rural:metro accessibility ratio was `r acc2(base_rm_med)`
at the reference specification and ranged from `r acc2(min(sens_summary$rm_med))`
(`r sens_lab_inline[[sens_summary$variant[which.min(sens_summary$rm_med)]]]`; deeper rural gap) to `r acc2(max(sens_summary$rm_med))` (`r sens_lab_inline[[sens_summary$variant[which.max(sens_summary$rm_med)]]]`;
shallower gap), while the median AIAN:White ratio moved only within
`r acc2(min(sens_summary$aw_med))`-`r acc2(max(sens_summary$aw_med))`
(reference `r acc2(base_aw_med)`) and stayed below 1.00 in every specification. The
production-resolution (500-m) grid reproduced the reference results almost exactly.
The per-subspecialty model-specification envelope (Appendix Table S2b) ranged from
`r acc2(sens_env_rm_min)` to `r acc2(sens_env_rm_max)` for the rural:metro ratio and
from `r acc2(sens_env_aw_min)` to `r acc2(sens_env_aw_max)` for the AIAN:White ratio;
`r if (sens_env_any_rural_reversal) "at least one rural:metro contrast crossed 1.00" else "no rural:metro contrast crossed 1.00"`, and
`r if (sens_env_any_aian_reversal) "the AIAN:White contrast crossed 1.00 only in near-parity specifications" else "no AIAN:White contrast crossed 1.00"`.
This insensitivity
of direction to the distance-decay weights is consistent with prior
enhanced two-step floating catchment area analyses, including studies of mental
health and of maternal-health services, in which access estimates were
likewise robust to varying the decay parameter [@Charlesworth2024; @Vadrevu2016].

```{r tableS2}

    `AIAN:White ratio (median)` = sprintf("%.2f", aw_med),
    `Rural < metro` = sprintf("%d/%d", n_rural, n),
```

*Appendix 3. Cell-level versus tract-level zero-access, 2020.*

The zero-access share reported throughout is defined at the census-tract level (the
share of a group's population in tracts whose *mean* modeled access is zero). As a
sensitivity comparison, a cell-level estimator was computed for 2020: for each
tract, the area-weighted fraction lying in 500-m grid cells with zero access,
aggregated by the tract's group population. The cell-level estimate exceeded the
tract-mean estimate for every group and subspecialty (median
+`r pp1(cz_med)` percentage points; maximum +`r pp1(cz_max)`), and the divergence
was largest for the lowest-access strata. Because both estimators assume
uniform population density within each tract, this comparison shows only that the
two definitions differ, not that either is the more accurate estimate of the true
burden; a dasymetric or block-level allocation would be needed to adjudicate.
Values agreed between the 500-m and 1,000-m grids to within 0.1 percentage point.

```{r tableS3}
czw <- cell_zero_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(group %in% c("Metropolitan","Rural","White, non-Hispanic",
                             "Am. Indian/Alaska Native")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(g = dplyr::recode(group, "Metropolitan"="Metro", "Rural"="Rural",
    "White, non-Hispanic"="White", "Am. Indian/Alaska Native"="AIAN"),
    cell = sprintf("%.1f", cell_zero_pct), tract = sprintf("%.1f", tract_zero_pct)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(subspec, g, cell_tract = paste0(cell, " / ", tract)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = g, values_from = cell_tract) |>
  dplyr::mutate(subspec = factor(subspec,
    levels = E2SFCA_SUBSPECIALTIES)) |>   # SSOT display order
  dplyr::arrange(subspec) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Subspecialty = full_name_disp[subspec], Metro, Rural, White, AIAN)
knitr::kable(czw, align = c("l","r","r","r","r"),
  caption = paste0("Appendix Table S3. Cell-Level vs Tract-Level Zero-Access ",
    "Share (%), 2020 (cell / tract)")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","condensed"),
                            font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "Each cell shows the cell-level zero-access share / the tract-level share (%). ",
    "Cell-level is the group-population-weighted mean of each tract's area fraction ",
    "in 500-m grid cells with zero modeled access; tract-level is the share in ",
    "tracts whose mean access is zero. Both estimators assume uniform within-tract ",
    "density, so the higher cell-level values reflect the definition, not evidence ",
    "that either is more accurate. ", abbr_note))
```

## eMethods S4: Enhanced two-step floating catchment area, algorithm, weights, and sensitivity {-}

Potential spatial accessibility was estimated with the enhanced two-step floating
catchment area (E2SFCA) method [@luoqi2009], an extension of the two-step floating
catchment area approach [@luowang2003] that is now widely applied to physician,
screening, surgical, and other health-service access [@Gilliland2019;
@Wurdeman2026; @Welch2024; @Campbell2025; @Charlesworth2024; @Utaka2026;
@Petzold2025; @Arora2025], and a recent systematic review situates them within the broader gravity-model family of potential spatial-access measures [@Stacherl2023]. Floating catchment methods were chosen over
crude provider-to-population ratios, which ignore where supply sits relative to
demand and capture a distinct dimension of access that binary distance or
travel-time thresholds undercount [@Nakamura2017; @SanchezCardenas2024;
@McCrum2022], and travel time along the road network was used
rather than straight-line distance, which overstates reachability where terrain or
road structure lengthens the true trip [@Ebinger2022].

The impedance choice is developed here because it conditions every estimate in the
paper. Three properties distinguish road-network drive time from a geodesic
(Euclidean or great-circle) radius. First, *validity of the catchment boundary*: a
geodesic buffer is a circle, and the set of places from which a physician can actually
be reached within a fixed time is not a circle. It is elongated along highways and
truncated at mountain ranges, large water bodies, roadless federal and tribal land,
and international borders, so a circle simultaneously includes places that cannot
reach the physician in time and excludes places that can. Comparisons of distance
types in accessibility research show that the resulting misclassification is not
symmetric and does not average out across a study area [@Apparicio2008]. Second,
*direction and location of the bias*: straight-line distance systematically
understates the trip, and it understates it most where the road network is sparse and
indirect. In a rural patient cohort, straight-line distance underestimated true road
distance by a mean of 31.9%, with individual discrepancies as large as 83.4 miles
[@Ludrosky2023]. Because the shortfall is concentrated in rural and mountainous
areas, a geodesic surface would be expected to inflate modeled rural access relative
to metropolitan access, and so to *compress* the rural-metropolitan ratios and
*understate* the zero-access shares that are this study's primary spatial outcomes.
The same argument applies to the American Indian or Alaska Native contrast, since
tribal lands are disproportionately served by low-speed and unpaved roads. We did not
recompute the surfaces under a Euclidean impedance, so this is a directional argument
from the metric's documented bias rather than a measured quantity; on that argument,
the disparities reported here are conservative with respect to the choice of metric.
Third, *consistency with the model's own parameters*: the enhanced two-step floating
catchment area method was formulated with travel-time zones and time-indexed
distance-decay weights [@luoqi2009], and the weights adopted here (and the published
values they match) are calibrated in minutes. Substituting mileage bands would break
the correspondence between the weights and the impedance they were estimated for,
which is a specification change rather than a robustness check, and it is for this
reason that the sensitivity analysis in Table S2 varies the decay function, the band
structure, the maldistribution penalty, and the grid resolution but retains drive
time as the impedance throughout.

The evidence base is not unanimous, and the boundary condition is worth stating
precisely. A nationwide U.S. comparison of driving distance, drive time, and
straight-line distance to community hospitals from more than 66,000 sampled locations
concluded that, for non-emergency hospital travel, the added precision from routing is
largely inconsequential [@Boscoe2012]. That conclusion is credible for the setting it
studied and does not transfer to this one. Community hospitals are numerous and
widely distributed, so the modal trip is short, and over short trips in a dense
network the ratio of road distance to straight-line distance approaches one and the
choice of metric barely moves the estimate. Obstetric-gynecology subspecialists are
neither numerous nor widely distributed: the relevant trips in this study extend to
60, 120, and 180 minutes, and for a large share of the rural population the nearest
subspecialist is reachable, if at all, over long distances on a sparse network. That
is precisely the regime in which routing and geodesic measures separate, and it is
consistent with the specialized-service and long-trip settings in which routed travel
time has been adopted in preference to distance [@Ebinger2022; @Weiss2020]. Taken
together, the geodesic approximation degrades as trip length rises and network density
falls, and this study sits at the unfavorable end of both.

Two consequences follow for interpretation. Drive-time estimates are not numerically
comparable with the distance-based accessibility literature, which is why the
gynecologic oncology comparison with county-level and 100-mile-radius estimates
[@Desjardins2023] is framed as a corroboration of pattern rather than of magnitude.
And drive time buys its validity at the cost of assumptions a geodesic measure does not
make, chiefly modeled rather than observed travel speeds, a single road-network
snapshot, and an assumption of private-vehicle travel; these are set out in eDiscussion S9 and are the
reason travel-time modeling is listed there among the sources of uncertainty the
reported intervals do not capture.

Demand within each catchment was weighted by empirically selected distance-decay weights across the four travel-time bands (weights
`r manifest_json$weights[["30"]]`, `r manifest_json$weights[["60"]]`,
`r manifest_json$weights[["120"]]`, and `r manifest_json$weights[["180"]]` for the
30-, 60-, 120-, and 180-minute zones); these band weights follow the
published E2SFCA formulation and match values in common use (the inner-band weights
are identical to those applied in recent screening-access studies). They approximate
a Gaussian falloff but were selected from prior empirical work rather than derived from an exact
Gaussian (a true Gaussian, sigma = 60 min, would place lighter weight on the 120-
and 180-minute bands and is examined as a sensitivity variant, Table S2). A slower
distance decay with a wider catchment is appropriate for specialized care that
patients travel farther to reach than primary care [@luoqi2009; @Campbell2025];
studies contrasting generalist and subspecialty access likewise assign
subspecialists materially wider catchments than primary care providers
[@Liu2026].
No single distance-decay function is empirically established as correct, and the
floating-catchment literature has called for finer spatial demand units and refined
decay functions than the coarse zone centroids and step weights used in most prior
work [@Hong2023; @Weng2025]; we therefore resolved demand on a fine grid, adopted
these conventional, empirically selected weights, and confirmed that the findings were insensitive
to this choice, to the catchment bands, and to the grid resolution in a sensitivity
analysis (Appendix Table S2). That sensitivity framework additionally supports a
Gaussian-derived versus purely zonal band-weight parameterization (a four-band
approximation, not a continuous distance function) [@McGrail2012], variable urban and
rural catchments that widen the effective catchment for rural populations
[@McGrail2009], and a modified two-step specification that penalizes suboptimally
configured supply (M2SFCA) [@Delamater2013]. The M2SFCA second application of the
distance weight is intentional and method-specific, not the inadvertent reuse of the
same weights in both steps cautioned against elsewhere [@Zhang2023trap]; a fully
dynamic variable-catchment implementation would expand each catchment until a
population and provider criterion is met rather than compositing separate fixed urban
and rural surfaces [@Luo2012var]. The four listed values are cumulative-band weights
$W_b$ (applied to the population reachable within band $b$); they enter the
computation as incremental band weights $w'_b = W_b - W_{b+1}$ (with $W$ beyond the
outermost band set to 0), which makes the cumulative-isochrone implementation
equivalent to a ring-based E2SFCA. In the first step, each physician location $j$
receives a provider-to-population ratio
$$R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_b w'_b\, P_{jb}},$$
where $S_j$ is the subspecialist supply at $j$ and $P_{jb}$ is the female population
reachable from $j$ within band $b$. In the second step, the accessibility at demand
cell $i$ is the band-weighted sum of the ratios of all physician locations whose
band-$b$ catchment contains $i$,
$$A_i = \sum_{j}\sum_{b} w'_b\, R_j .$$
Supply $S_j$ is the count of distinct active subspecialists (unique National
Provider Identifiers) whose practice location maps to $j$. A quality-control check
confirmed that every physician had exactly one active practice location in each
study year, so supply reflects one physician-equivalent per physician and no
multisite duplication occurred; had a physician held multiple locations the
estimator would have counted them fully at each, so fractional (1/$k$) allocation
would be required only for an extension of the cohort to multisite practice
(Limitations). Accessibility
is a relative index expressed as subspecialists per 100,000 women; it is not a raw
physician-to-population density and is not directly numerically comparable with
distance-based accessibility scores [@Desjardins2023]. We also express it as a
Spatial Access Ratio normalized to the national population-weighted mean of 1.00,
with values above 1 indicating better-than-average spatial access [@Wan2012spar];
the absolute per-100,000 index is retained alongside it so that normalization cannot
conceal changes in the absolute national supply-demand balance.

A structural property of the two-step method is important for interpretation.
Because the same band weights enter both steps, the population-weighted mean of the
accessibility surface over *all* demand reduces algebraically to the total supply
divided by the total population,
$$\frac{\sum_i P_i A_i}{\sum_i P_i}=\frac{\sum_j R_j\sum_i w'_{ij}P_i}{\sum_i P_i}=\frac{\sum_j S_j}{\sum_i P_i},$$
which we verified numerically (the national means in Table 1 equal
subspecialist counts per 100,000 women to within 0.02%). The *national*
mean is therefore a **standardized supply-per-population index** and carries no
spatial information; the across-subspecialty ranking it induces is the
workforce-size ranking. Spatial variation is expressed only in the *distribution* of
the surface, the rurality and race/ethnicity contrasts, the share of the population
outside the modeled catchment, and geographic inequality, which we accordingly treat
as the primary spatial outcomes. National means and their ranking are reported as
standardized workforce measures, not as spatial accessibility.

## eResults S5: Disparities across all subspecialties {-}

Viewed across all seven specialty groups, the disparity pattern was consistent
(Figure 4). In 2020, rural women had lower potential accessibility than
metropolitan women for every subspecialty, by as much as
`r pp1(abs(rural_worst_pct))`% for `r full_name[rural_worst]` and by at least
`r pp1(abs(rural_min_pen))`% even for the least affected subspecialty. Areas where
American Indian or Alaska Native women lived had materially lower accessibility (by
at least 10 percent) than areas where non-Hispanic White women lived for
`r n_aian_worse` of the seven specialty groups (and lower accessibility, to any
degree, in all seven). By contrast, areas where Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native
Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander women lived generally had higher modeled
accessibility than areas where non-Hispanic White women lived, reflecting their
greater concentration in metropolitan areas where subspecialists practice, a pattern
of potential proximity that, as discussed below, does not imply equivalent realized
access or outcomes. These spatial patterns were robust to the modeling assumptions:
across the alternative specifications (Appendix Table S2), the rural lower-access
pattern held for all `r sens_n`
subspecialties under every specification, and the rural and race contrasts moved in
magnitude but never reversed in direction (Appendix Table S2).

```{r fig_equity_hm}

# also vendored in twostep/scripts/). See docs/FIGURE_PROVENANCE.md.
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig_equity_heatmap.jpg"))
```
**Figure 4.** Potential accessibility for lower-access strata relative to their
reference strata in 2020, across all seven specialty groups. Each cell is the percent
difference in 2020 population-weighted accessibility between a stratum and its
reference stratum *within* that subspecialty:
red = at least 10% lower access, blue = at least 10% higher, gray = within ±10%.
Reference groups: rurality, metropolitan; race and ethnicity, non-Hispanic White.
Within-subspecialty relative contrasts facilitate comparison across subspecialties
of differing scarcity, but should be interpreted cautiously where absolute
accessibility is low (for example, complex family planning and pediatric and
adolescent gynecology), because relative differences become unstable at very small
baseline values. Enhanced two-step floating catchment area access per 100,000
women;
tract-level population-weighted; contiguous United States. AIAN, American Indian or
Alaska Native; NHOPI, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander.

## eResults S6: Persistence of disparities over time {-}

Rural and area-level racial disparities persisted across the decade (Figure 5; Appendix
Table S1). Over `r first_year`-`r primary_last`, the metropolitan-to-rural
gynecologic oncology accessibility ratio narrowed by
`r sprintf("%.3f", abs(go_ratio_trend[["slope"]]))` per year
(`r fmt_p_txt(go_ratio_trend[["p_ols"]])`; Newey-West
`r fmt_p_txt(go_ratio_trend[["p_hac"]])`), and the gynecologic oncology zero-access
share in areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women lived declined by
`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(gtr("GO","AIAN")$slope_pp_yr))` percentage points per year
(`r fmt_p_txt(gtr("GO","AIAN")$p_ols)`; Newey-West
`r fmt_p_txt(gtr("GO","AIAN")$p_hac)`) while remaining highest among race/ethnicity strata in
every year. Directions were unchanged under autocorrelation-robust inference,
although with only 10 annual estimates the trend tests are imprecise (Appendix
Table S1).
