## eResults S7: Access deserts across subspecialties {-}

The magnitude of inaccessibility depended strongly on subspecialty scarcity
(Figure 6; Table 3). The rural zero-access share ranged from about `r pp1(rural_zero_min)`% for `r rural_zero_min_sub`
to about `r pp1(rural_zero_max)`% for `r rural_zero_max_sub`, and was consistently highest in areas where American Indian or Alaska
Native women lived (Table 3). These tract-level, travel-time patterns parallel
the
county-level, distance-based gynecologic oncology access disparities reported by
Desjardins and colleagues [@Desjardins2023].

## eResults S8: Change in accessibility by subspecialty {-}

Descriptive changes in potential accessibility from `r first_year` to
`r last_year` were geographically heterogeneous across subspecialties (Figure 7).
This `r first_year`-`r last_year` endpoint comparison, in which `r last_year` is
provisional, is distinct from the `r first_year`-`r primary_last` modeled trends
reported above. Nationally, population-weighted accessibility increased most for
`r full_name[top_gain$subspecialty]` (`r pp1(top_gain$rel_change_pct)`%), and
`r full_name[decliners$subspecialty[1]]` was the only subspecialty to decline
(`r pp1(decliners$rel_change_pct[1])`%); however, both gains and losses were
spatially concentrated rather than uniform across the country. Figure 7 shows the
absolute cell-level change, while the facet labels report the national relative
change over the same `r first_year`-to-`r last_year` endpoint window (not the
primary `r first_year`-to-`r primary_last` values reported in Table 1).

## eDiscussion S9: Limitations {-}

Several limitations temper interpretation. First, and most important, the same
total-female-population denominator was applied to all seven specialty groups. Because
the subspecialties serve different populations, pediatric and adolescent gynecology
serves children and adolescents; maternal-fetal medicine, reproductive
endocrinology, and complex family planning serve predominantly reproductive-aged
patients; and urogynecology and reconstructive pelvic surgery serves an older
population, the large across-subspecialty differences in the standardized index
reflect workforce size and clinical scope as well as access, and the rates should
not be read as directly comparable measures of clinical adequacy; age-specific,
within-specialty denominators are a priority for future work, alongside supply- and
demand-adjusted catchments that model service-specific capacity and age-specific
need [@ShaoLuo2022] and distance-decay functions empirically calibrated from observed
patient-flow data rather than prespecified [@KhosraviKazazi2026; @FloridaV2SFCA2026]. Second, the measure
reflects potential (modeled) rather than realized access and does not capture
practice capacity, appointment availability, insurance acceptance, or patient
travel behavior; in particular, because higher-socioeconomic-status patients more
readily overcome distance by traveling to distant centers, a spatially uniform
potential-access measure may understate realized disadvantage for lower-income and
rural populations [@Yilma2023]. Relatedly, drive time is a better impedance than
geodesic distance (eMethods S4) but is itself modeled, and it carries assumptions a
straight-line measure does not make. Travel times are modeled rather than observed:
absent an applied historical traffic profile *[the routing engine's speed
configuration to be confirmed by the authors]*, the isochrones represent typical
rather than time-specific conditions and do not vary with time of day, day of week,
weather, seasonal road closure, or ferry and mountain-pass schedule, so they will
understate travel burden in congested metropolitan corridors and in winter conditions
at high elevation and latitude. To the extent that unrepresented congestion is the
larger of these, it favors metropolitan areas, and the reported rural-metropolitan gap
is conservative on that axis. A single OpenStreetMap snapshot was applied to all study years, a
deliberate choice that isolates cohort change from road-extract change (Methods) but
that consequently attributes no accessibility gain to roads actually built during the
study period. The model also assumes private-vehicle travel and therefore does not
represent women without reliable access to a car or those who depend on public
transit, paratransit, or informal rides, for whom the effective catchment is smaller
than the modeled one; multimodal floating-catchment formulations that route separately
by car and by transit address this directly and are a natural extension
[@Langford2016]. Isochrones were also built to the physician's practice-location
coordinate, so travel is measured to a point rather than to a clinic entrance,
parking, and check-in. Third, the reported ACS intervals quantify only ACS sampling
uncertainty and are not comprehensive confidence intervals. We added a deterministic
model-specification envelope for the 2020 rural:metro and AIAN:White ratios
(Appendix Table S2b), so the sensitivity to catchment bands, distance decay,
maldistribution penalty, and grid resolution is quantified rather than left only as
prose. That envelope still omits stochastic uncertainty from physician
ascertainment and activity classification, geocoding, multiple practice locations,
practice capacity, and road-network travel-time modeling; Monte Carlo propagation of
supply, activity, geocoding, and parameter uncertainty through the model is a natural extension
[@Park2023], and potential edge effects at the international borders and coastlines
(providers and population outside the United States were unavailable) could not be
captured [@Gao2017]; however, a sensitivity analysis across the alternative
specifications left the
direction of the rurality and race disparities unchanged (Appendix Table S2; the
national mean and its ranking are invariant to these choices by the conservation
property and are not a robustness result). Fourth, the zero-access metric is defined at the tract level (the share of
a group living in tracts with zero mean modeled access) and may undercount people
in zero-access locations within partially served tracts. A cell-level
estimator for 2020 (the area-weighted share of each tract that lies in grid cells
with zero access, weighted by the tract's group population) gave
higher zero-access shares than the tract-mean metric (median
+`r pp1(cz_med)` percentage points across groups and subspecialties, and up to
+`r pp1(cz_aian_max)` for American Indian or Alaska Native and +`r pp1(cz_rural_max)`
for rural women; Appendix Table S3). However, both estimators assume uniform
population density within each tract, so this difference does not establish that the
tract-mean metric understates the true burden; it shows only that the two
definitions diverge, and resolving which is more accurate would require a dasymetric
or block-level population allocation, which we did not perform. Relatedly, spatial associations can depend on the choice of areal unit
(the modifiable areal unit problem); we resolved demand at a fine scale (census
tract allocated to a 500-m grid) to limit this, but stratified estimates could
differ under coarser units [@ElKhoury2024]. The area-weighted allocation also
conserves population without validating its within-tract placement: it assumes
uniform density within each tract, which is least tenable in large rural and tribal
tracts, and a dasymetric or block-level allocation would better locate women;
mass conservation prevents loss but does not by itself certify spatial precision.
Fifth, race-alone and Hispanic-origin groups do not form a mutually
exclusive classification, so between-group contrasts are among separately defined
groups; moreover, the broad American Community Survey categories mask substantial
within-group heterogeneity (for example, across Asian-origin subgroups), and finer
disaggregation, shown elsewhere to reveal disparities that pooled categories
conceal, is a priority for future work [@Greenberg2023]. These stratified estimates
are ecological: they are computed at the census-tract level from group-specific
population denominators and describe the accessibility of the areas where each group
lives, not the realized access of individual patients, and within-tract residential
patterns may differ by group. Sixth, overlapping ACS
5-year estimates and serially correlated cohorts
make ordinary least-squares trend inference optimistic; we therefore report
Newey-West autocorrelation-consistent P values alongside the ordinary least-squares
values (Appendix Table S1), although with only 10 annual estimates these remain
imprecise, and the maternal-fetal medicine trajectory is nonlinear (decline then
rebound), which a single linear slope summarizes incompletely. Moreover, the
2019-2020 census-tract vintage change falls within the trend window; a
subgroup-specific seam test (2020 cohort held fixed, each subgroup recomputed under
the 2010- and 2020-vintage frameworks; Methods) found the pure vintage shift to be
small (median `r sprintf("%.2f", seam_zero_med)` percentage point in the zero-access share, and
at most `r pp1(seam_ra_max)` for the rural and American Indian or Alaska Native
series), so the subgroup trends crossing the boundary are not attributable to the
vintage change, with the exception of the Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander
series, whose smaller population produced the largest shift
(`r pp1(seam_zero_max)` percentage point) and which is already limited by the
exclusion of Hawaii. Seventh, the most recent year (`r last_year`) is
right-censored and is reported provisionally. Eighth, we summarized accessibility
descriptively and did not model residual spatial autocorrelation, which
spatially explicit approaches address directly [@McCrum2022]. Finally, the analysis
was restricted to the contiguous United States because road-network routing cannot
represent the air and water travel on which access in Alaska, and in much of Hawaii,
depends; the closest prior urogynecology-access study likewise restricted its main
analysis to the continental United States for the same reason [@Schmidt2024]. Alaska
is therefore a boundary of the modeling framework rather than an omission:
quantifying access there would require an air- and maritime-inclusive travel model,
not the road-network isochrones on which this entire study is built. This
exclusion bears most on the American Indian or Alaska Native category, whose very
name includes Alaska Natives: our estimates pertain to the contiguous-U.S. members
of that group and omit Alaska-resident Alaska Natives, who face distinct and
frequently non-road access barriers that are typically more severe. Because the
excluded population is among the least geographically served, the lower access
observed for areas where American Indian or Alaska Native women live is, if anything,
conservative with respect to the full national population. The exclusion of Hawaii is equally relevant to the
Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander results, which should likewise be read as
pertaining only to the contiguous-U.S. members of that group.

## Reproducibility record (supplement, not part of the typeset manuscript) {-}

*The following provenance metadata is provided for the reproducibility repository
and peer review; it is not intended for the submitted/typeset article.*

```{r provenance, results="asis"}
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "- **Run:** `%s` (git `%s`)\n",
  "- **Allocator:** %s / `%s` (mode %s; module sha256 `%s`)\n",
  "- **Headline source:** %s\n",
  "- **Cells:** %d specialty-year national rows (7 specialties × 11 years)\n"),
  manifest_json$run_id, substr(manifest_json$git_sha, 1, 8),
  manifest_json$allocator$method_id,
  manifest_json$allocator$population_allocator,
  manifest_json$allocator$mode,
  substr(manifest_json$allocator$module_sha256, 1, 16),
  manifest_json$headline_source, nrow(national_tbl)))
```

*All scientific values above are inline R expressions evaluated from the canonical
run objects at render time; none are hardcoded in prose.*

**Figure provenance.** Every figure was generated in the upstream isochrones pipeline
from the frozen run `e2sfca_20260712_190734` and staged into this repository; the
generator script, data input, and build date for each are recorded in
`docs/FIGURE_PROVENANCE.md` (machine-readable `manuscript/figures/FIGURE_PROVENANCE.csv`)
and in a comment above each figure's chunk. Figure 1 (`fig0_level2020.jpg`) was
regenerated 2026-08-02 to remove the in-image title, subtitle, and footnote caption.
Filenames do not track figure numbers (for example Figure 5 is `fig4_gotrends.jpg`);
resolve by the provenance table.
